title: Shanghai's 'Audacious' New Opera House Just Opened Its Doors—and a Gravity-Defying Staircase—to the Public

sections.title: Conversation 1
sections.scene: A graduate student and her professor discuss a proposed public lecture on opera house architecture.

script.en: Professor, do you have a moment? I'm organizing next month's public lecture series for the architecture society, and I'd like your advice on a speaker.
Of course. Who did you have in mind?

I was thinking of inviting Dr. Lin, the cultural historian who wrote that book on waterfront performance venues. Her work on how public buildings either welcome or exclude ordinary citizens seems perfect for our theme.
That's a strong choice. She's rigorous but accessible. Have you considered what angle she might take? Audiences here are mostly students and local residents, not specialists.
I thought she could focus on the tension between prestige and accessibility. Many new opera houses are architectural landmarks, yet people assume they're only for the wealthy.

Exactly. That assumption is worth challenging. But be careful not to let the talk become a simple celebration of bold design. The interesting question is whether a striking staircase or an open lobby actually changes who feels entitled to walk in.
So you'd want her to address the gap between symbolic openness and real participation?
Precisely. And she should probably mention that free entry to a building doesn't automatically create a new audience for the art performed inside. Access is a start, not a solution.
That's a useful distinction. I'll ask her to include concrete examples, perhaps comparing European and Asian cases.
Good. Also, keep the Q&A session generous. Students often ask the most revealing questions about cultural exclusion.
I'll schedule thirty minutes. One more thing: should we charge for tickets? We need to cover the honorarium.
I'd suggest a small suggested donation rather than a fixed fee. It signals openness while still supporting the series. And advertise through community centers, not just the university list.
That makes sense. Thank you. I'll send her the invitation this afternoon.

sections.title: Passage
sections.scene: A news commentary on how cultural buildings balance spectacle and public access.

script.en: Across the world, cities are competing to build cultural landmarks that do more than house performances. A new generation of opera houses, museums and concert halls is being designed to attract ordinary residents, not just ticket-holding elites who can afford premium seats. Architects increasingly treat staircases, rooftops and lobbies as public spaces, inviting people to enter without purchasing a seat or committing to a full evening program. This approach reflects a broader shift in urban policy. Governments hope that iconic buildings will boost tourism, stimulate local business and project an image of cultural sophistication to both visitors and investors. Yet critics point out that architectural openness does not automatically produce social inclusion. A spectacular staircase may draw crowds for photographs, while the performances inside remain expensive and unfamiliar to many citizens. Researchers who study cultural participation argue that access has two dimensions. The first is physical: Can people reach the building, and do they feel welcome to enter? The second is psychological: Do they believe the art presented there is meant for them? Removing entrance fees addresses the first dimension but leaves the second largely untouched. Without education programs, community partnerships and diverse programming, a landmark may remain a beautiful shell, and some cities have responded with practical measures. They schedule free open rehearsals, collaborate with schools and invite local amateur groups to perform. These efforts are less photogenic than a gravity-defying staircase, but they may do more to change who actually walks through the doors. The lesson is that cultural buildings succeed as civic destinations only when design is matched by sustained outreach.

sections.title: A New Opera House Tests the Meaning of Openness
sections.passage:
Shanghai's newest opera house opened this week, presenting a bold architectural profile and a soaring spiral staircase that links the street to a rooftop stage and observation deck. The nearly 1.6 million square-foot building contains three auditoriums with a combined capacity of 4,200 seats. Its stages were designed to host everything from traditional opera to classical symphonies and experimental productions.

The primary performance space, a 2,000-seat hall called Harmony Hall, is described by its architects as a finely tuned instrument that combines advanced theatre systems with carefully calibrated acoustics. A second venue, the 1,200-seat Soar Theatre, was conceived with baroque and classical opera in mind. The smaller Open Stage, which offers panoramic riverfront views, prioritizes flexibility through changing stage and seating configurations. Throughout, the main hall is a stark white space filled with natural light and sharp red accents.

Visitors need no ticket to enter the building or to explore its architectural features. That philosophy of openness is embodied by the massive exterior staircase, which rises from the riverfront and spirals upward to form the roof. It is intended to connect existing walkways with an open-air observation deck, gathering spaces and a stage. The staircase alone resembles a large public sculpture, evoking a traditional Chinese fan, a swirling dance movement, piano keys and the flow of the Huangpu River.

Yet the building's architects insist that a cultural institution must answer to its surroundings and to the people who use it. "Buildings like opera houses inevitably create thresholds through walls, doors and ticketed programs," co-founder Kjetil Thorsen told Dezeen. "We see it as our responsibility to challenge those thresholds and make the building as much a civic destination as a performance venue." That ambition, however, raises a question: whether a dramatic staircase and an open lobby can genuinely alter who feels entitled to walk in.

The inaugural season, running from October through February 2027, will feature 82 performances, including ballet from Russia's Eifman Ballet and the American Ballet Theatre, a Beethoven cycle from Staatskapelle Berlin, and traditional Chinese operas such as The Peony Pavilion and Dream of the Red Chamber. Such programming signals prestige, but prestige alone may not dissolve the psychological distance that keeps many residents away from the art inside.

Shanghai, a financial hub of roughly 25 million people, has recently opened several major cultural venues, from the Museum of Art Pudong to the West Bund Grand Theatre. The new opera house thus joins a wider civic effort. As Thorsen told CNN, accessibility is about daring to go in, and about feeling invited even if you are not the average opera goer. Whether that feeling spreads beyond the photogenic staircase will depend on sustained outreach as much as on design.

long_sentences.en: It will feature 82 performances, including ballet numbers from Russia’s Eifman Ballet and the American Ballet Theatre ; a Beethoven cycle from Staatskapelle Berlin , one of the world’s leading orchestras; and traditional Chinese operas, called xiqu , including The Peony Pavilion and Dream of the Red Chamber .

“It’s not only about the glass walls and the doors, but it’s about being attracted to the space as you come in, and you feel that even if you’re not the average opera goer, you’re invited in.” Christian Thorsberg is an environmental writer and photographer from Chicago.

“A cultural building, any building for that matter, must respond to its surroundings, the people who use it, the performers it serves, and the city it becomes part of,” Kjetil Thorsen, the co-founder of Snøhetta, tells Dezeen ’s Lizzie Crook.
